newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - May 6.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - May 6.

text.p: - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- CITY REGULATOR WARNS BANKS OF CREDIT DERIVATIVES RISK

Vicki Fitt, the executive director for financial risk at the Securities and Futures Authority has warned banks they should examine the dangers before becoming involved in the credit derivatives market. The regulator has proposed that credit derivatives are treated more flexibly than the bank of England, allowing banks to hold less capital, helping avoid c.d. risks. Investment bankers are said to have welcomed the SFA treatment as it leaves room in the market for development.
-- INSIDER DEALING PROBE IN GERMANY'S SAP

German business software company SAP is the subject of an insider trading investigation by German prosecutors. The Frankfurt state prosecutors office has said SAP could provide the most "far-reaching case" of insider trading in three years. Management and supervisory board members totalling over 100 are the main focus of the extensive investigation which begun following information provided by the federal supervisory office for securities trading.
-- TRIAL RUN FOR EURO FAILS TO IMPRESS BERLINERS

The EC held a trial Euro run in Germany recently, in an attempt to convince the skeptical German population of the currency's merit. German opinion polls continue to show that two- thirds of the population are opposed to economic monetary union, demonstrated by the refusal by many Germans to use the new currency in its trial run. 1.3 million coins were minted, with another 15,750 collectors euro coins also put up for sale.
-- EMU COULD HIT MARKET JOBS AND PROFITS

The Financial Times (Preparing for Emu) column examined the issue of Emu and the sense of urgency it is placing on investment bankers following a report published by the London Investment Banking Association which focused on the impact of Emu on capital markets. Some bankers worry rationalisation of the European bond and currency markets could come at the expense of their jobs and many traders may be secretly hoping that Emu will fail, thereby safeguarding their jobs.
-- LEGAL WRANGLE MAY DELAY GAS BILL CUTS BY A YEAR

If UK gas regulator Ofgas rejects the Monopolies and Mergers Commission report into tough price controls for British Gas' Transco GSA.L pipeline monopoly, it may be almost a year before consumers see sharp cuts in gas bills. It is not certain this will be the outcome, but is solely what executives are calling the "worst case scenario", which would lead to a judicial review that could last nearly one year. Immediate price cuts of 28 pounds sterling on a 350 pound sterling yearly bill have been proposed by Ofgas.
-- PENTIUM II COMING TO A SCREEN NEAR YOU

Computers manufactured by sixteen different companies containing Intel II, the latest and most powerful processor from Intel, are set to be launched in Britain. Compaq, IBM and Gateway 2000 are among the computer companies who have implemented the device which has been labelled the most important product launch for Intel since 1994. The Pentium II equips the business market with "visual" computing facilities such as multimedia applications, 3-D graphics and video-conferencing. The machines will be available to the public in December.
-- TELECOMS OPERATORS WARNED ON INTERNET THREAT

Werner Knetsch, head of global telecoms consultants Arthur D Little, has warned telecoms firms that ignore the threat posed to their business by the Internet may face loss of customers and revenues to the computer industry. Knetsch listed Microsoft and Netscape as planning to capture the voice and fax markets key to telecoms operators' business. The warning follows a report last week from Phillips Tarifica which predicted that after 2000 leading telecoms operators would lose millions of dollars in international revenues because of low voice call costs over the Internet.
-- RIVALS IN DISPUTE OVER DNA CHIP PATENTS

US biotechnology company Affymetrix is to challenge Oxford University in a challenge over one of the most powerful medical innovations of recent years. The company, 34 per cent owned by Glaxo Wellcome, is disputing ownership of a DNA chip - the device for rapidly analysing human genetic makeup using silicon chips containing bits of DNA.
-- DRUG COMPANY BUYS CLINICS

Gambro, the Swedish healthcare company, is to pay 1.6 billion sterling for Vivra, the US healthcare operator which owns more than 260 kidney dialysis clinics in 28 US states as well as selling management services to doctors and others co-ordinating kidney disease management.
-- HOECHST WARNS ON IMPACT OF SHAKE-UP

German pharmaceuticals and chemicals group Hoechst has posted pre-tax profits of DM831 million ($480.8 million) for the first quarter of 1997, an increase of 9 per cent on the same period last year. However, the results were below market expectations and the group warned that, under its radical restructuring, sales and profits in 1997 would be lower than last year.
